claims.text: The target nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially form a homogeneous solid solution.
High configurational entropy governs retention of structural and chemical stability from 473 K to 1923 K.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Local variations in metal-metal bonding impede atomic diffusion.
Impeded atomic diffusion suppresses phase segregation under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
Controlled atmospheres minimize external contamination during thermal cycling.
High configurational entropy lowers the overall free energy of the solid solution.
The entropy-induced reduction in free energy suppresses phase separation at high temperatures.
Local disparities in bonding energy create barriers to atomic diffusion.
Atomic diffusion would otherwise lead to elemental segregation.
The combined entropy and bonding effects preserve chemical uniformity over a broad temperature range.
The combined entropy and bonding effects preserve structural uniformity over a broad temperature range.
After cycling between 473 K and 1923 K, the nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
After thermal cycling, the nanoparticles will show minimal phase segregation relative to their initial state.
After thermal cycling, the nanoparticles will show minimal chemical redistribution relative to their initial state.
The prediction is restricted to precisely equiatomic nanoparticles tested without uncontrolled oxidation.
Significant composition deviations, surface contamination, or uncontrolled environmental factors may change the stability outcome.
The proposed mechanism lacks direct experimental evidence spanning the full temperature range through 1923 K.

contradictions.description: The material scope includes equal or near-equal atomic ratios, whereas the boundary states that the prediction holds only for precisely equiatomic nanoparticles.
